title: Who Pays for America's Research and Development?
gist: An infographic brief tracking U.S. R&D funding from 1957 to 2023 shows a full inversion: government funded roughly two-thirds of national R&D at the dawn of the Cold War versus less than a fifth today, while industry now funds about three-quarters, forcing the Pentagon to court and adapt commercial innovation rather than drive it.

themes.theme: Inversion of who funds US R&D

insights.claim: At the time of Sputnik in 1957, the U.S. government funded nearly two-thirds of the nation's research and development, much of it defense-related, driving the technological frontier that the private sector then followed.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Establishes the historical baseline against which today's funding inversion is measured.
insights.quote: It funded nearly two-thirds of the nation’s research and development — much of it for defense — defining the early Cold War.
insights.locator: When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957

insights.claim: Today industry funds roughly three-quarters of U.S. research and development while the federal government's share has fallen below one-fifth, a complete inversion of the 1957 split.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the public-to-private funding shift shaping where cutting-edge defense-relevant technology now originates.
insights.quote: Today, that arrangement has been inverted. Industry now funds roughly three-quarters of U.S. research and development, while Washington’s share is less than a fifth.
insights.locator: Today, that arrangement has been inverted

insights.claim: Because the technological frontier increasingly emerges from commercial labs rather than government programs, the Pentagon must now court and adapt private-sector innovation instead of directing it.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Reframes the Pentagon's posture toward commercial tech firms as one of adaptation and courtship rather than command, relevant to defense-tech vendor relationships.
insights.quote: Because the cutting edge increasingly emerges from commercial labs, the Pentagon must now court and adapt innovation, rather than drive it.
insights.locator: Because the cutting edge increasingly emerges

themes.theme: Defense's shrinking share of a still-large federal R&D pie

insights.claim: Defense research and development made up about 85 percent of total federal R&D funding in the Sputnik era, compared to roughly 49 percent today.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies defense's declining share of a federal R&D budget that itself is a shrinking piece of total national R&D.
insights.quote: Defense research and development comprised about 85 percent of total funding in the Sputnik era, compared to roughly 49 percent today.
insights.locator: The infographic’s second layer also explores

insights.claim: The decline in defense's share of federal R&D reflects a surge in civilian funding, mainly NIH biomedical research, rather than an actual Pentagon retreat, and defense remains the dominant funder when the lens is narrowed to engineering.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Corrects a naive reading of the defense-share decline as budget cuts; the Pentagon's engineering R&D dominance is intact.
insights.quote: this dynamic reflects less a Pentagon retreat than a surge in civilian (mainly National Institutes of Health biomedical research) funding. If the lens is narrowed to engineering, the Defense Department remains the dominant funder.

themes.theme: Who performs the work versus who funds it

insights.claim: Measured by who actually performs the research rather than who funds it, industry's share is even larger, about 77 percent in 2023, because companies also carry out federally funded work under contract.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Shows industry's operational dominance in R&D execution is even greater than its funding share suggests, reinforcing the Pentagon's dependence on contractors.
insights.quote: Measured by performance, industry’s share is larger still (about 77 percent in 2023), because companies also carry out federally funded work under contract.
insights.locator: Although we didn’t discuss who performs research
